title: “JUDGE NOT!” — THE TWO WORDS JESUS SPOKE THAT MILLIONS HAVE MISUNDERSTOOD
paragraphs: “JUDGE NOT!” — THE TWO WORDS JESUS SPOKE THAT MILLIONS HAVE MISUNDERSTOOD
Did Jesus Really Command Christians Never to Judge Anyone? Or Have We Turned His Warning Against Hypocrisy Into an Excuse to Avoid the Truth?

What if one of the most quoted teachings of Jesus has become one of the most misunderstood—and what if that misunderstanding is quietly destroying our ability to recognize sin, confront deception, and love people the way Christ actually commanded?
Someone is destroying their marriage through an affair.
A friend sees the warning signs. Knows what is happening. Knows a family is being torn apart.
But when someone finally speaks up, the response comes quickly.
“Who are you to judge me? Didn't Jesus say, ‘Judge not’?”
And suddenly, the person trying to stop the destruction becomes the villain.
The betrayal is overlooked.
The warning is condemned.
And the words of Jesus are used to silence the very truth that could lead someone to repentance.
But there is another side to this story.
A young woman walks into church after years of addiction, broken relationships, and decisions she desperately wishes she could undo.
She is trying to find God.
She barely knows how to pray anymore.
Before anyone asks her name, someone notices her tattoos. Another notices her clothes. Someone whispers about her past.
She came hoping to encounter grace.
Instead, she encounters a courtroom.
And the people who should have pointed her toward the Savior make her feel as though she must become acceptable before she can approach Him.
Two situations.
Two terrible distortions.
In one, people use “judge not” to protect sin from correction.
In the other, people use religious judgment to keep wounded sinners away from grace.
And somewhere between those two extremes stands Jesus Christ.
Not confused.
Not contradicting Himself.
Not compromising holiness.
Not abandoning mercy.
The question is whether we are willing to listen to everything He actually said.
Because Jesus never gave us permission to celebrate sin.
And He never gave us permission to crush sinners.
He called us to something far more difficult: truth without hypocrisy, discernment without arrogance, and correction shaped by love.
And that changes everything.
In Matthew 7:1, Jesus says:
“Judge not, that ye be not judged.” (KJV)
The Greek text reads:
Μὴ κρίνετε, ἵνα μὴ κριθῆτε.
Transliteration: Mē krinete, hina mē krithēte.
A straightforward translation is:
“Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”
The verb κρίνετε (krinete) comes from κρίνω (krinō), which can mean to judge, evaluate, distinguish, or pronounce judgment, depending on the context.
And context is exactly what we must not ignore.
If we stop at Matthew 7:1, we can make Jesus sound as though He forbade every moral evaluation, every correction, and every distinction between righteousness and wrongdoing.
But Jesus did not stop speaking after verse one.
He continued:
“For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.” (Matthew 7:2, KJV)
Then He gave an unforgettable picture.
A man notices a tiny speck in his brother's eye.
He approaches, ready to correct him.
But there is a problem.
The man doing the correcting has a beam of wood in his own eye.
Imagine that scene.
Someone walking around with a massive plank protruding from his face, confidently offering delicate eye surgery to someone else.
It is almost comical.
Until we recognize ourselves.
We notice another person's impatience while excusing our cruelty.
We condemn someone's dishonesty while carefully hiding our own.
We criticize someone's marriage while neglecting the person God entrusted to us.
We expose another believer's pride while secretly enjoying the feeling of being spiritually superior.
And Jesus says:
“Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye.” (Matthew 7:5, KJV)
Read those final words again.
“Then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye.”
Jesus did not say to leave the speck there forever.
He said to deal with your own obstruction first.
That is the part many people miss.
The problem was not that someone wanted to help his brother see clearly.
The problem was that he was trying to correct another person while refusing to confront his own sin.
Jesus was exposing hypocrisy, not abolishing moral discernment.
He was confronting self-righteousness, not commanding moral blindness.
He was teaching that before you approach another person's brokenness, you must be willing to stand honestly before God about your own.
Because a person who has genuinely repented approaches another sinner differently.
There is less arrogance.
Less eagerness to humiliate.
Less pleasure in exposing failure.
More trembling.
More compassion.
More awareness of how desperately we all need mercy.
The closer you come to understanding the holiness of God, the harder it becomes to pretend that you are morally superior to everyone around you.
And yet, this does not make sin less serious.
It makes correction more humble.
Consider something Jesus said in John 7:24:
“Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.” (KJV)
The Greek reads:
μὴ κρίνετε κατ᾽ ὄψιν, ἀλλὰ τὴν δικαίαν κρίσιν κρίνατε.
Transliteration: Mē krinete kat' opsin, alla tēn dikaian krisin krinate.
The meaning is clear:
“Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment.”
Notice the contrast.
Jesus does not simply repeat, “Never judge.”
He commands His listeners to judge rightly.

The context matters. In John 7, Jesus was responding to people who misunderstood and criticized His healing on the Sabbath. He challenged their inconsistent reasoning and called them to a judgment based on what was right rather than on superficial appearances.
Matthew 7 and John 7 do not contradict each other.
They correct different errors.
Matthew warns against hypocritical judgment.
John calls for righteous judgment.
Together, they show us that the issue is not whether Christians should ever distinguish right from wrong.
The issue is whether our judgment is truthful, humble, consistent, and submitted to God.
And this is where things become uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we call something “discernment” when it is actually gossip.
Sometimes we call something “righteous anger” when it is personal resentment.
Sometimes we call something “defending the faith” when we are really defending our ego.
And sometimes we call something “love” when we are simply afraid to tell the truth.
Jesus confronts all of it.
Think about the people He encountered.
He spoke with a Samaritan woman whose personal life was deeply complicated.
In John 4, He did not pretend her circumstances were different from what they were.
He knew the truth about her relationships.
But He did not treat her as disposable.
He offered her living water.
The conversation that exposed her past also opened the door to her testimony.
She went back to her community and told people about the One who knew her life.
What a Savior.
He knew what she had done.
And He still spoke to her.
He did not need to deny the truth to offer grace.
And He did not need to humiliate her to reveal it.
Now consider Zacchaeus.
A chief tax collector, wealthy and despised, standing among people who regarded him as a sinner.
Jesus looked up into the tree and called him by name.
He entered his home.
And Zacchaeus responded with a remarkable declaration about giving to the poor and restoring what he had taken unjustly.
Jesus announced that salvation had come to that house (Luke 19:1–10).
Notice the order of the encounter.
Jesus did not treat Zacchaeus as beyond the reach of mercy.
But neither did the encounter leave Zacchaeus celebrating the injustice of his former life.
Grace reached him.
And his response showed transformation.
Biblical grace does not require pretending that sin is harmless. It brings sinners to the Savior who can forgive and change them.
This is why the Gospel is so much more powerful than either condemnation or compromise.
Condemnation says, “You are too filthy to come near.”
Compromise says, “You do not need to change.”
Jesus says:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.” (Mark 1:15, KJV)
The Greek word translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε (metanoeite), from μετανοέω (metanoeō).
It speaks of repentance—a change of mind and orientation that, in the biblical call to repentance, involves turning from sin toward God.
Repentance is not merely feeling embarrassed because someone discovered what you did.
It is not simply regretting consequences.
It is responding to God's truth with a changed heart that begins to bear fruit in a changed life.
And that change is not something we purchase with good behavior.
It is the fruit of God's grace at work in us.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds both truths together: we are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
We are not saved because we successfully cleaned ourselves up.
We are saved by the grace of God in Christ.
But the grace that saves us does not teach us to make peace with the sin that enslaved us.
Titus 2:11–12 says God's grace teaches us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts.
Grace is not permission to remain in darkness.
Grace is God's undeserved favor bringing us into a new life.
And sometimes that new life begins with a painful conversation.
A friend telling you the truth you do not want to hear.
A spouse confronting a pattern that is destroying trust.
A pastor gently correcting a dangerous misunderstanding.
A brother or sister in Christ saying, with tears rather than superiority, “I love you too much to pretend this is not hurting you.”
Proverbs 27:6 says:
“Faithful are the wounds of a friend; but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.” (KJV)
Not every painful word is faithful, of course.
Cruelty does not become righteous simply because it contains a fact.
But neither does every uncomfortable correction become hatred.
Sometimes love warns.
Sometimes love confronts.
Sometimes love refuses to applaud what is destroying someone.
And sometimes the most loving words are the ones spoken with a trembling voice.
“I am worried about you.”
“This is not what Scripture teaches.”
“You need help.”
“You do not have to keep hiding.”
“Please come back to Jesus.”
But there is a crucial difference between confronting someone's sin and pretending to know the final condition of their soul.
We can recognize behavior that contradicts Scripture.
We cannot see the human heart with God's perfect knowledge.
We can warn someone about a destructive path.
We cannot appoint ourselves the final Judge of their eternal destiny.
We can speak what God has revealed.
We must not claim knowledge He has not given us.
James 4:12 reminds us:
“There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy: who art thou that judgest another?” (KJV)
And 1 Corinthians 4:5 warns against pronouncing judgment prematurely, before the Lord brings hidden things to light.
That means humility is not optional.
You may know what someone did.
You may not know everything they suffered.
You may know the words they spoke.
You may not know every motive behind them.
You may see the chapter they are living through.
You cannot see the whole story God is writing.
That is why Christians must never confuse biblical discernment with omniscience.
We are servants of Christ.
We are not Christ.
And the moment we forget that, even our defense of truth can become infected with pride.
Paul addressed this balance directly in Galatians 6:1:
“Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.” (KJV)
The Greek word translated “restore” is καταρτίζετε (katartizete), from καταρτίζω (katartizō).
It carries the sense of putting something into proper condition, repairing, or restoring.
That is an extraordinary word to use when addressing a believer caught in wrongdoing.
Paul does not tell the church to enjoy the scandal.
He does not command them to build their identity around another person's disgrace.
He calls them to restoration.
And he adds a warning to the person doing the restoring:
Consider yourself.
Remember your own vulnerability.
Remember that you, too, can be tempted.
The goal is not to win an argument against a fallen brother.
The goal is to seek his restoration.
Not to make someone feel small so you can feel righteous.
Not to collect evidence for public humiliation.
Not to turn a person's worst moment into entertainment.
But to help bring someone back toward faithfulness to Christ.
This does not mean every situation should be handled privately or that serious wrongdoing should be concealed.
Jesus gives a process for addressing sin between believers in Matthew 18:15–17, beginning with a private conversation and allowing further steps when necessary.
Other biblical passages address serious public wrongdoing and the responsibilities of church leaders.
And when abuse, exploitation, violence, or criminal conduct is involved, protecting victims and involving appropriate authorities must never be replaced by pressure to remain silent.
Restoration is not the same as avoiding accountability.
Forgiveness is not the same as pretending trust has already been rebuilt.
And mercy must never become a shield for someone who continues harming others.
The church should be a place where repentance is welcomed, truth is honored, the vulnerable are protected, and wrongdoing is addressed with integrity.
Not a place where powerful people escape correction while wounded people are told to endure more suffering.
That is not biblical mercy.
That is a distortion of it.
And Jesus had strong words for religious hypocrisy.
In Matthew 23, He rebuked religious leaders who burdened others while failing to practice the righteousness they publicly demanded.
He did not condemn them for caring about holiness.
He condemned the hypocrisy that corrupted their religious lives.
Think about that.

Some of the strongest warnings in the Gospels are directed not toward people openly admitting their need for mercy, but toward those who used their appearance of righteousness to conceal spiritual corruption.
That should make every one of us examine ourselves.
Especially those of us who teach.
Especially those of us who correct others.
Especially those of us who speak publicly in the name of Jesus.
Because knowing the right verses does not automatically mean we are applying them with the right heart.
You can quote Scripture accurately and still wield it cruelly.
You can defend a true doctrine while behaving in a way that contradicts the character of Christ.
You can expose someone else's sin while secretly refusing to surrender your own.
And the answer is not to abandon Scripture.
The answer is to submit ourselves to it first.
Before you correct someone, ask whether you are seeking their good or your own vindication.
Before you share someone's failure, ask whether you are protecting others or simply spreading humiliation.
Before you pronounce someone hopeless, remember how patient God has been with you.
Before you say, “I would never do that,” remember Peter.
Peter, who promised loyalty.
Peter, who insisted he would never deny Jesus.
Peter, who heard the rooster crow after denying the Lord three times.
Imagine that moment.
The courtyard.
The questions.
The fear.
The denial.
And then the sound.
A rooster crowing into the darkness.
Luke 22:61 records that the Lord turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered Jesus' words.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
Scripture does not tell us every thought passing through Peter's mind.
But it tells us enough to understand that this was a moment of devastating failure.
The man who had spoken so confidently had fallen so terribly.
Now imagine if Peter's story ended there.
Imagine if the final word over his life was coward.
Hypocrite.
Failure.
Unworthy.
But after the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, the risen Christ questioned him about his love and entrusted him with responsibility to care for His sheep.
Jesus did not rewrite history by pretending Peter had never denied Him.
He restored Peter without making his denial the final definition of his life.
That is grace.
Not the denial of sin.
Not the erasure of responsibility.
But the mercy of the risen Savior reaching a broken disciple and calling him forward.
And perhaps that is the part of this article you needed most.
Because maybe you have been the person holding the stone.
Quick to criticize.
Slow to listen.
Able to identify everyone else's failures while refusing to confront your own.
Maybe you have damaged someone with words you called “truth.”
Maybe you have confused spiritual maturity with always having something negative to say.
And today, Jesus is calling you to put down your pride.
Or perhaps you are the person everyone keeps talking about.
The one whose past follows you into every room.
The one who has repented but still hears whispers.
The one who wonders whether the church will ever see you as anything other than the worst thing you did.
You know you were wrong.
You are not asking anyone to call darkness light.
You just wish someone would believe that God is still working in you.
Hear this carefully.
Your sin is serious.
But your sin is not more powerful than the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
Not after we became impressive.
Not after our reputations were repaired.
Not after everyone approved of us.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
That is the scandal of grace.
The holy Son of God gave Himself for people who could never earn His mercy.
At the cross, God did not simply overlook evil as though it did not matter.
Christ bore our sins, as 1 Peter 2:24 declares.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the astonishing love of God.
And through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, we have a living hope.
So no, the Gospel does not say that everyone is automatically innocent.
It says guilty sinners can be forgiven through Jesus Christ.
It does not say repentance is unnecessary.
It calls us to turn to God.
It does not say holiness is irrelevant.
It teaches us to follow the One who saved us.
And it does not give forgiven people permission to become merciless toward others.
Remember the parable of the unforgiving servant in Matthew 18:21–35.
A servant receives extraordinary mercy for a debt he cannot repay.
Then he turns around and refuses mercy to a fellow servant who owes him far less.
Jesus uses that story to expose the wickedness of receiving mercy while refusing to extend it.
How easily we become that servant.
We want God to remember His grace when He looks at our failures.
But we want Him to remember His judgment when He looks at the failures of people who hurt us.
We want patience for our own spiritual growth.
But immediate perfection from everyone else.
We want forgiveness for the things we regret.
But sometimes struggle to believe others can genuinely change.
And suddenly Matthew 7 becomes deeply personal.
The question is no longer merely, “Am I allowed to judge?”
It becomes:
“Am I treating other sinners like someone who knows how much he has been forgiven?”
That question reaches beyond social media arguments.
It enters our homes.
Our marriages.
Our friendships.
Our churches.
Our private conversations.
Our comment sections.
The way we speak about someone who has fallen.
The way we respond when someone confronts us.
The way we handle a believer who is struggling.
The way we treat a person who does not yet believe what we believe.
And it demands more than a clever theological answer.
It demands a changed heart.
Because righteous judgment is not merely about identifying the correct moral conclusion.
It also requires that we respond in a way consistent with God's revealed character.
Ephesians 4:15 calls believers to speak the truth in love.
Truth matters.
Love matters.
Neither cancels the other.
Truth without love can become a weapon.
Love without truth can become an excuse for leaving someone in danger.
But truth spoken in love seeks the person's ultimate good before God.
It is willing to say what is difficult.
And willing to say it with humility.
It does not rejoice in another person's downfall.
It does not turn repentance into a spectacle.
It does not demand that someone earn the right to hear the Gospel.
And it does not promise peace by hiding what God calls sin.
Perhaps you are reading this while wrestling with a difficult situation.
Someone you love is making choices that concern you.
You do not want to be judgmental.
But you do not want to be silent.
What should you do?
Begin with prayer.
Examine your own life.
Make sure your concern is grounded in Scripture rather than personal preference, rumor, or wounded pride.
Listen before assuming you know the entire story.
When correction is warranted, speak truthfully and gently.
Choose an appropriate setting.
Be willing to help carry the burden instead of merely identifying it.
And remember that you cannot force another person's repentance.
You can be faithful.
You can be compassionate.
You can speak.
You can pray.
But you cannot replace the work of the Holy Spirit.
Nor should you confuse someone else's refusal to listen with permission to become cruel.
And if you are the one being corrected, do not automatically assume that every uncomfortable word is persecution.
Sometimes the person confronting you is mistaken.
Sometimes they are acting hypocritically.
But sometimes they are telling you something you desperately need to hear.
Ask God for the humility to distinguish between those possibilities.
Proverbs 12:1 reminds us that loving instruction is connected with loving knowledge.
Correction can hurt.
But refusing all correction can harden the heart.
And the heart that refuses to be corrected may eventually become incapable of recognizing how far it has wandered.
That is a frightening place to be.
Not because God has stopped calling sinners to repentance.
But because pride can make His warnings sound like insults.
There is another truth we must face.
One day, every human being will stand before God.
Romans 14:10–12 reminds us that we will each give an account of ourselves to Him.
That means the person you criticize is accountable to God.
And so are you.
The person who hurt you is accountable to God.
And so are you.
The person who hides behind “judge not” to justify sin is accountable to God.
And the person who uses Scripture to humiliate others is accountable to God.
None of us will stand before Him as the ultimate authority over everyone else's life.
We will stand as people who need the righteousness and mercy of Jesus Christ.
And that should change how we live right now.
Because the cross leaves no room for boasting in our own moral superiority.
But it also leaves no room for treating sin as something harmless.
At Calvary, we see how desperately we need forgiveness.
And how costly our redemption was.
This is why the message of Gospel Warrior will never be that your past does not matter.
Your choices matter.
Sin matters.
Repentance matters.
Truth matters.
But your past does not have to be the final chapter of your story.
Jesus Christ can forgive what you cannot undo.
He can restore what sin has shattered.
He can transform the heart that has grown cold.
He can teach the proud to become humble.
He can teach the wounded to forgive.
He can teach the fearful to speak truth with courage.
He can take a person who once used Scripture to condemn others and teach that person to use Scripture faithfully, with gentleness and love.
And He can take someone who once resisted every warning and give that person a heart willing to repent.
That is not self-improvement dressed in religious language.
That is the transforming grace of God.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
Not a new person because everyone finally approves of you.
Not a new person because you have successfully hidden your past.
A new creation in Christ.
And that is where the entire question about judgment finally leads us.
Not to a world where no one is ever corrected.
Not to a church where everyone is constantly condemned.
But to a Savior who calls sinners to repentance, offers forgiveness through His blood, and teaches His people to walk in truth and love.
So the next time someone says, “Jesus told us never to judge,” remember the whole counsel of Scripture.
Remember Matthew 7:5.
Remove the beam from your own eye.
Remember John 7:24.
Judge with righteous judgment.
Remember Galatians 6:1.
Restore with gentleness.
Remember Ephesians 4:15.
Speak the truth in love.
Remember James 4:12.
God is the ultimate Judge.
And above all, remember Jesus Christ.
The One who never sinned.
The One who knew the truth about humanity.
The One who confronted hypocrisy, welcomed repentant sinners, healed the broken, and gave His life to redeem those who could not save themselves.
If this message has exposed something in your own heart, do not rush past that conviction.
Perhaps there is someone you need to apologize to.
Someone you judged without understanding.
Someone you humiliated when you should have helped.
Or perhaps there is a sin you have been defending by accusing everyone who confronts you of being judgmental.
Bring it to Jesus.
Not with excuses.
Not with religious performance.
With repentance.
With honesty.
With faith in His mercy.
First John 1:9 reminds believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
You do not have to keep pretending.
And you do not have to keep running.
The Savior who calls you to repentance is the Savior who died and rose again so that sinners might be reconciled to God.
If this article reached a place you have been hiding, I want to invite you into a moment of spiritual honesty.
You do not need to tell the internet every detail of your story.
Sometimes a simple request for prayer is enough to remind someone else that they are not struggling alone.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who desperately needs this message.
Someone who has been wounded by religious condemnation.
Someone who has confused grace with permission to keep sinning.
Someone who is drifting away from Christ because no one has lovingly told them the truth.
That simple act can help carry biblical encouragement into conversations and homes this page may never reach on its own.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to win an argument.
But because you care about their soul.
There may come a day when you are tempted to judge harshly—or when you are afraid to speak a necessary truth—and you need to return to these Scriptures.
We are not building a community of people who pretend to have perfect lives.
We want to point imperfect people to the perfect Savior.
And for those who desire to help this ministry continue and reach further, I want to extend a personal invitation.

Gospel Warrior's work takes time, care, resources, and ongoing commitment. Every article, biblical reflection, discipleship resource, and message of encouragement is an opportunity to place Scripture before someone who may be searching for hope.
For believers who choose to give in this way, it can be part of their personal generosity and offering to God.
No payment can purchase God's favor.
Our desire is to make biblical nourishment, encouragement, and opportunities for spiritual growth accessible to people who need them.
The mission is not to make people dependent on a ministry.
It is to keep pointing people to Jesus.
Because He is the One who saves.
He is the One who forgives.
He is the One who transforms.
And He is the One worthy of the glory.
So here is the truth I hope stays with you long after you close this article.
Jesus did not command you to stop recognizing sin.
He commanded you to stop pretending you are above the need for grace.
He did not call you to abandon discernment.
He called you to exercise it righteously.
He did not call you to celebrate another person's failure.
He called you to pursue truth, holiness, mercy, and restoration.
And He did not come merely to make condemned people feel better about remaining in darkness.
He came to save sinners and bring them into His marvelous light.
So put down the pride.
Put away the excuses.
Stop using “judge not” to silence every warning.
Stop using “righteous judgment” to justify every cruel word.
Look at the cross.
Remember the mercy you have received.
And when you encounter someone who has fallen, remember that the Gospel is not the announcement that fallen people must remain fallen forever.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for sinners, rose victorious, and calls us into new life through repentance and faith.
Before you become the voice that reminds someone of their worst sin, remember the Savior who refused to let your worst sin be the end of your story.
